items.summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.38

Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon. I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse.

Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price, and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires.

The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up:

So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen.

Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st.

I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high.

I dropped Argon from my Gemini 4 comparison grid - here's the new Gemini 4 lineup, where the Neon pelicans do look better than Hydrogen and worse than Carbon:

As I've done with several recent models, I also fired the following prompt against Gemini 4 Neon on "extra" effort level in Google Antigravity:

Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data

Here's the result.

items.title: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost
items.story_key: story|title:introducing harness adapters adapt your favorite model to your harness to improv
items.content_excerpt: Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution. Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination. Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time. Our earlier work ( multi-harness RL , harness adapters ) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations. We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2 , OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6 . The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol: Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop , SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM 's agent and environment classes, slime 's custom rollout functions, or ART 's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. items.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
items.summary: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

items.title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
items.summary: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedural ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity, or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short \emph{lessons} from the agent's own trajectories, one to three per episode. It then consolidates those lessons into a smaller set of \emph{guidelines}, where each guideline records how many lessons it merged. At inference the agent receives either all guidelines or a selected subset. The pipeline ships in the open-source altk-evolve library and is deployed in IBM's CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate platform. We report what we learned building, measuring, and productizing it. Our primary instrument is the AppWorld benchmark, across models spanning 40--92\% baseline task completion. The central finding is that the right amount of memory is a property of the model, not the memory. A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are added. DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 points of task completion and +16.1 points of scenario completion with its full 191-guideline set. A weak model gains less from the same full set than from a small selected subset. gpt-oss-120b starts at 39.9\% task completion. It reaches 51.2\% with all 199 of its guidelines but 55.4\% (mean of two runs) with a selected subset of about 29. Around that result we report what went wrong: a high-support guideline that backfired, provenance silently dropped during consolidation, a swallowed API error that failed every task while producing a plausible log, and a baseline confound that nearly produced a misleading comparison with a prior method. We distill these into recommendations for teams deploying agent memory.

items.title: Your Software Factory Needs a Bill of Materials | Daniel Meppiel
items.summary:
Developers are about to write skills instead of code, and Microsoft's Daniel Meppiel argues the software factory that runs them needs versioning, a bill of materials and signed receipts before enterprises will trust it.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/7jw

Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Simon Maple sits down with Daniel, of Microsoft's Global Black Belt team and creator of APM (Agent Package Manager), to dig into why teams keep rebuilding the same skills, how to version a skill when the change is in its behavior rather than a method signature, and why skills can only ever be guidance while security controls stay deterministic. Then stay for Daniel's full DevCon talk, Version Your Factory, Not Just Your Code, on agent contracts, signed receipts and the evidence a regulated enterprise needs before it auto-merges.

What we cover:
– Why developers will write skills and prose instead of code
– Why teams keep rebuilding the same skills, and the case for a shared skill catalog
– Testing and versioning skills with evals: when is a change a major version?
– APM, lock files and an agent bill of materials for your software factory
– Skills are guidance, security controls are deterministic
– Daniel's AI DevCon talk: agent contracts, signed receipts and auto-merging on evidence

items.title: vllm v0.34.0
items.summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Important

These changes can break existing setups.

Change What to do PR
Model Runner V1 removed Remove VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor. #63373
Default --block-size is 64 (was 16) Pass --block-size 16 to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. #63231
Extensible KV cache on by default; gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 In most cases it's now best to not set gpu_memory_utilization. This should provide maximum kv cache capacity while avoiding runtime OOMs. Use it to share a GPU with other processes or when extensible kv cache is disabled. #56492
ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. -rocm72 is no longer published. #61939
huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 required Also requires tokenizers >= 0.23.3 and timm >= 1.0.30. #64779
QuTLASS / fp_quant removed fp_quant checkpoints no longer load. #65230
Marlin W4A8 removed Use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG instead of VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE. #65542
Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed — #64287

All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in the full changelog.

New models

Model Notes PR
Mistral Large 4 1T total / 52B active, FP8 and NVFP4. Runs on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350. #64534
MiniMax-M3.1-Flash Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft #64111
NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and /v1/audio/transcriptions #64282
Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview BF16 and NVFP4, ripple reasoning and tool parsers #65745
Zyphra ZAYA1 ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview #65302
Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 DASH sparse attention #64016
Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio #65826, #65827, #65828
NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 ASR and X↔En translation #64215
Ming3-ASR #63585
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin #65005

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

Performance

Improvement Hardware Gain PR
Step5 NVFP4 MoE on TRTLLM-Gen 4×GB200 up to 1.95× decode #65152
GLM-5.3-Flash DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE NVIDIA 1.6× output throughput vs DEP4 #60895
Muse Spark Open specialized decode (opt-in) GB300 1.5× single-stream decode #64077
Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (default) GB200 GLM-5.3 TTFT 1.24–1.40× faster at 32K–128K #63956
KV-balanced MLA decode for Kimi-K3 (opt-in) GB300 1.34–1.59× decode attention #63638
Qwen3.5 on breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) NVIDIA 3.0–8.8% lower decode ITL #51012
FlyDSL decode monokernel, Muse Spark Open DSpark 8×MI355X +35–57% interactivity at conc. 1–8 #63440

AMD ROCm

  • Release images and wheels are ROCm 10.0 only (#61939).
  • MoRI EPv2 via --all2all-backend mori (#61361).
  • Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435).
  • TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418).

Serving and operations

  • Checkpoint/restore (CRIU + cuda-checkpoint) through /checkpoint/prepare, /checkpoint/status and /checkpoint/restore, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570).
  • Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down: dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370).
  • Best-effort NUMA binding on by default (#61258).
  • Opt-in cache-aware admission ordering (#54625).
  • Rust frontend: stateless Responses API (#63902) and n > 1 (#65625).

Install

Python wheels

Platform Install
CUDA 13.0 (PyPI) pip install vllm
CUDA 13.0 (uv) uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto
ROCm 10.0 pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.34.0/rocm100
XPU uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/0.34.0/xpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu --index-strategy unsafe-best-match

Docker images

Platform Image Short alias

CUDA 13.0 + DeepEP over AWS EFA vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0-efa vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-efa
ROCm 10.0 vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-rocm

XPU vllm/vllm-openai-xpu:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-xpu

latest tags work the same way (e.g. vllm/vllm:latest-rocm). The default CUDA image now includes the AWS EFA userspace (libfabric, aws-ofi-nccl). The -efa image adds DeepEP built for EFA and routes NCCL over EFA by default (#65576).

The Assets section below has the source tarball and the CUDA 13.0 (x86_64, arm64), CPU (x86_64, arm64, macOS) and XPU (x86_64) wheels.

Full changelog

Model support

    • DSpark, DCP/PCP, NIXL P/D and HiSparse.
  • Other new models:

    • Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe with MTP and DFlash2 (#64282, #64944).
  • DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1

    • Decoder replay graphs share the model graph pool: prefill graph memory 15.52 → 9.88 GiB per rank on GB200 (#63155).
    • fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant 3.5× faster, prefill 6% faster (#63540).
    • DSpark/MTP memory savings of about 512 MiB per GPU (#63996).
    • Engram host tables shared across DP ranks (#62359).
    • DeepGEMM sparse MQA logits on the FP8 indexer cache (#62011).
    • Packed multi-image vision encoding, 1.6–2.6× (#65030).
    • LoRA on the language model, compressor and wo_a layers (#57245, #64880).
    • DSpark with PCP (#61994); PCP with PP or DP (#63098).
    • Fixes: sparse prefill in FULL CUDA graphs (#59986), prefill memory budgeting (#63047), MTP embedding under PP (#65816), DeepSeek-V3.2 PP (#59961).
  • GLM
    • GLM-5.3-Flash: DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE (#60895), adaptive verification (#60229), row-strided QKV into FlashKDA (#61614).
    • GLM-5.3 FP8 MoE sorted-A TMA on H200, 6.0–7.6% E2E throughput (#64760).
    • FP8 KV cache for DSpark and DFlash drafts (#63841, #64612, #65553).
    • FP32 indexer MQA logits restored for GLM-5/GLM-5.3/HY-V4, with new --attention-config.indexer_logits_dtype (#64580).
    • Fused KDA convs fix stale weights after RL refit (#60991).
  • Muse Spark

items.title: From tasks to goals
items.summary: LangChain CEO and Co-founder Harrison Chase shares how we're moving from task-specific agents to goal-focused agents. Learn more.
items.story_key: story|title:from tasks to goals
items.content_excerpt: As agents become more powerful, we’re moving from giving them tasks to giving them goals. Under the hood, this move from tasks to goals consists of two more practical shifts: This is changes what an agent does, what it needs, how its built, and we interact with it. Previously, the user would specify tasks. Now, the user specifies a goal, and the agent iterates towards that goal by deconstructing into tasks, doing some of them, updating the task list, etc. The agent needs to be good at brainstorming and selecting different tasks, which requires new context engineering and prompting strategies. It needs to be somewhat creative - and varied - in brainstorming potential tasks (if it keeps on suggesting the same tasks over and over again, that’s not great). Practical consideration: you need some way to see what tasks the agent is doing (e.g. a to-do list), as well as prompting for the agent to be creative in coming up with tasks When you give an agent task, you largely have an idea of what tools it will call. When you give it a goal - you don’t really know what tools it will call, and you may not even know what tools it will need to call. Practical consideration: you need more controls over what tools an agent can or cannot call When you give an agent a task, you’re naturally in the loop. If you don’t provide all the information up front, its easy for the agent to ask follow up questions in chat. When you give an agent a goal - it may be running in the background and need to get clarification on certain points. It needs a way to ask questions to humans - whether through Slack or a dedicated UI. Practical consideration: you need a mechanism for a background agent to ask you for clarification The agent needs to know how its doing as it progresses towards a goal. This could either be by checking in on a metric to see if it is improving, or by getting explicit feedback from a human on how its doing. The more closely tied to a metric, the better in some sense (easy for it to track automatically!) but its never wise to blindly optimize a metric, so explicit human feedback may be the best thing. This is why its important to design goals in a way where its easy to give feedback. You can have both metrics for the agent to drive towards, and a way to get feedback from users. items.title: A$^2$-VLA: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Policies to New Tools through Agentic Affordance Discovery
items.summary: Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting the manipulation strategy accordingly. The key challenge is to discover the common affordances that contribute to task completion across different tools and verify whether they support new tools in performing similar work. We present A$^2$-VLA, a tool-adaptation framework that combines an embodied agent with a VLA policy. It treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct, test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent reconstructs the scenes in simulation and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features: functional regions and their key geometric properties. It develops affordance-extraction skills and refines both the features and skills through autonomous experiments in the reconstructed scenes. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable skill library for unseen tools. Finally, A$^2$-VLA uses encoded functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $π_{0.5}$ backbone during training and inference. Evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and real-robot task success on unseen tools. Our method achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances. On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A$^2$-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage points over $π_{0.5}$.

items.title: ClosureBench: A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions
items.summary: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.

  • Fixed claude mcp add and claude mcp remove with project scope deleting other top-level keys from .mcp.json, such as $schema or another tool's servers
  • Fixed /export overwriting an existing file without asking: the dialog now asks, and /export <name> keeps the file and says to run /export
  • Fixed a command you had allowed still running after you pressed Stop, when the approval arrived after a restart, in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions with no feature flags loaded
  • Fixed Enter closing /teleport's load error screen
  • Fixed a click followed by Enter in /plugin installing or disabling a plugin
  • Fixed a half-typed ! command running on an extra Enter after the usage limit menu
  • Fixed some --disallowedTools rules with parentheses in their content

items.title: An updated Clairic and Clairic-flash are now open-weight, from the new Workers AI Superintelligence team
items.summary: Clairic graduates from preview, while Clairic-flash joins the repertoire on Workers AI. We’re doing an open-weight release for both extraction models.
items.story_key: story|variant:flash|title:an updated clairic and clairic flash are now open weight from the new workers ai
items.content_excerpt: Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community. Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face . We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef , Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community. Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic. Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request. The model is still incredibly fast and cheap. From the evals below, you can see how our newer versions of Clairic have greatly improved on extraction across text, images, PDFs, and more. There are no public extraction benchmarks yet, but we ran our internal evals for other emerging extraction models on the market, such as Liquid AI’s D1.2 (pipelined with Apple Vision for optical character recognition) and Scaledown’s Extract .
